This manuscript examines how humans walk over uneven terrain and use vision to decide where to step. There is a huge lack of evidence about this because the vast majority of locomotion studies have focused on steady, well-controlled conditions, and not on decisions made in the real world. The author team has already made great advances in this topic by pioneering gaze recordings during locomotion, but there has been no practical way to map the gaze targets, specifically the 3D terrain features in naturalistic environments. The team has now developed a way to integrate such measurements along with gaze and step tracking. This allows quantitative evaluation of the proposed trade-offs between stepping vertically onto vs. stepping around obstacles, along with how far people look to decide where to step. The team also introduces several new analysis techniques to accompany these measurements. They use machine learning techniques to examine whether retinocentric depth helps predict footholds and develop simulations to assess possible alternative footholds and walking paths. The technical achievement is impressive.

This study addresses several real-world questions not normally examined in the laboratory. First, do humans elect to walk around steeper footholds rather than over them? Second, is there a quantifiable benefit to walking around, such as allowing for a flatter path? Third, does visual depth of terrain contribute to selection of footholds? Fourth, are there scale effects, where for example a tall adult can easily walk over an obstacle that a toddler must walk around. One might superficially answer yes to all of these questions, but it is highly nontrival to answer them quantitatively. As for the conclusions, my feelings are mixed. I find strengths in answers to two of the questions, and weaknesses in the other two.

Strengths:

I consider the evidence strongest for the first of the main questions. The results show subjects walking with more laterally deviating paths, measured by a quantity called "tortuosity," when the direct straight-ahead paths appear to have steeper ups and downs (Fig. 9). The measure of straight-ahead steepness is fairly complicated (discussed below), but is shown to be well correlated with tortuosity, effectively predicting when subjects will not walk straight ahead.

There is also good evidence for the third question, showing that retinocentric depth is predictive of chosen footholds. Retinocentric depth was computed by a series of steps, starting with scene capture to determine a 3D terrain mesh, projecting that mesh into the eye's perspective, and then discarding all but the depth information. This highly involved process is only the beginning, because the depth was then used to train a neural network classifier with chosen footholds. That network was found to predict footholds better than chance, using a test set independent from the training set, each using half the recorded data. The results are strong and are best interpreted along with a previous study (Bonnen et al. 2021) showing that subjects gaze nearer ahead on rougher terrain, and slightly more so when binocular vision was disrupted. Depth information seems important for foothold selection.

As an aside, humans presumably also select footholds and estimate depth from a number of monocular visual cues, such as shading, shadows, color, and self-motion information. Interestingly, the terrain mesh and depth data here were computed from monocular images, suggesting that monocular vision can in principle be predictive of both depth and footholds. Binocular human vision presumably improves on monocular depth estimation, and so it would be interesting to see whether binocular scene cameras would predict footholds better. In an earlier review, I had suggested other avenues for exploration, but these are not weaknesses so much as opportunities not yet taken. I believe much could be learned from deeper analysis of the neural network, and future experiments using variations of this technique.

There is much to be appreciated about this study. I was impressed by the overarching outlook and ambitiousness of the team. They seek to understand human decision-making in real-world locomotion tasks, a topic of obvious relevance to the human condition but not often examined in research. The field has been biased toward well-controlled, laboratory studies, which have undeniable scientific advantages but are also quite different from the real world. The present study discards all of the usual advantages of the laboratory, yet still finds a way to explore real-world behaviors in a quantitative manner. It is an exciting and forward-thinking approach, used to tackle an ecologically relevant question.

I also appreciate the numerous technical challenges of this study. The state of the art in real-world locomotion studies has largely been limited to kinematic motion capture. This team managed to collect and analyze an unprecedented, one-of-a-kind dataset. They applied a number of non-trivial methods to assess retinocentric depth, simulate would-be walking paths and steepness, and predict footholds from neural network. Any of these could and probably will merit individual papers, and to assemble them all at once is quite beyond other studies I am aware of. I hope this study will spur more inquiries of this type, leveraging mobile electronics and modern machine learning techniques to answer questions that were previously only addressable qualitatively.

Weaknesses:

Although I am highly enthusiastic about this study, I was not entirely convinced by the evidence for the second and fourth questions. Some of this is because I was confused by aspects of the analysis, limiting my understanding of the evidence. But I also question some of the basic conclusions, whether the authors indeed proved that (from Abstract, emphasis mine) "[walkers] change direction TO AVOID taking steeper steps that involve large height changes, instead of [sic] choosing more circuitous, RELATIVELY FLAT paths." (I interpret the "of" as a typo that should have been omitted). I think it is more objective to say, "walkers changed direction more when straight-ahead paths seemed to have steeper height changes."

I say "seemed" because it is unknown whether humans would have experienced greater height changes if they walked straight ahead (the second main question). The comparison shown is between human tortuous paths taken and simulated straight-ahead paths never experienced by human. Ignoring questions about the simulations for now (discussed below), it is not an apples-to-apples comparison, say between the tortuous paths humans preferred and straight-ahead paths they didn't. The authors determined a measure of steepness, "straight path slope" (Fig. 9), that predicts when humans circuitously, but that is the same as the steepness that humans would actually experience if they had walked straight ahead. That could have been measured with an appropriate control condition, for example asking subjects to walk as straight ahead as they can manage. That also would have eliminated the need for simulations, because the slope of each step actually taken could simply have been measured and compared between conditions. Instead, two different kinds of simulations are compared, where steeper paths are fully simulated, and the circuitous paths are partially simulated but partially based on data. It seems that every fifth circuitous step coincides with a human foothold, but the intervening ones are somewhat random. I don't find this especially strong evidence that the chosen paths were indeed relatively flatter. I would prefer to be convinced by hard data than by unequal simulations.

I also have trouble accepting "TO AVOID" because it implies a degree of intent not evident in the data. I suppose conscious intent could be assessed subjectively by questionnaire, but I don't know how unconscious intent could be tested objectively. I believe my suggested interpretation above is better supported by evidence.

My limited acceptance is due in part to confusion about the simulations. I was especially confused about the connection between feasible steps drawn from the distribution in Figure 7, and the histograms of Figure 8. The feasible steps have clear peaks near zero slope, unity step length, and zero step direction (let's call them Flat). If 5-step simulations of Figure 8 draw from that distribution, why is there zero probability for the 0-3 deg bin (which is within {plus minus}3 deg due to absolute values)? It seems to me that Flat steps were eminently available, so why were they completely avoided? It seems that the simulations were probabilistic (and not just figurative) random walks, which implies they should have had about the same mean as Figure 7 but a wider variance, and then passed through absolute value. They look like something else that I cannot understand. This is important because the RELATIVELY FLAT conclusion is based on the chosen walks apparently being skewed flatter than random simulated walks. I have trouble accepting those distributions because Flat steps were unaccountably never taken by either simulation or human. (This issue is less concerning for Figure 9, because one can accept that some simulation measure is predictive of tortuosity even if the measure is hard to understand).

I was also confused why Figure 7 distances and directions are nearly normally distributed and not more uniform. The methods only mention constraints to eliminate steps, which to me suggests a truncated uniform distribution. It is not clear to me why the terrain should have a high peak at unity step length, which implies that the only feasible footholds were almost exclusively straight ahead and one step length away. It is possible that the "feasible" footholds are themselves drawn from a "likely" normal distribution, perhaps based on level walking data. It could be argued that simulated steps should be performed by drawing from typical step distributions for level ground, eliminating non-viable footholds, and then repeating that across multiple steps. That would explain the normality, but it is not stated in the Methods, and even if they were "feasible and likely" it would not explain the distributions of Figure 8.

I had some misgivings about the fourth question, where Figure 10 suggests that shorter subjects had greater correlation between straight-path slope and tortuosity than taller ones, who tended to walk straighter ahead. I agree with the authors' rebuttal to my previous review that "the data are the data" but I still have doubts. Now supplied as suggested by another reviewer, Figure 18 provides more detail of the underlying data, with considerably lower correlations. I now suspect that Figure 10 benefits from some statistical artifacts due to binning and other operations, and the weaker correlations of Fig. 18A are closer to reality. I am rather suspicious of correlations of correlations (Figure 18B), which lose some statistical grounding because the second correlation treats all data on equal footing, effectively whitewashing the first correlations of their varying significance (p-values 0.008 to 1e-9).

Furthermore, I am also unsure about Figure 10's comparison of tortuosity vs. straight path slope against leg length. Both tortuosity and straight path slope are already effectively dimensionless and therefore already seem to eliminate scale. It is my understanding that the simulated paths were recomputed for each subject's parameters, and the horizontal axis, slope, is already an angular measure that should affect short and tall people similarly. Shouldn't all subjects equally avoid steep angles, regardless of their dimensional height? If there is indeed a scale effect, then I would expect it to be demonstrated with a dimensional measure (vertical axis) that depends on leg length.

I certainly agree with the hypothetical prior that tall adults walk straight over obstacles that shorter adults (or children) walk around. But I feel that simpler tests would better evidence, perhaps in future work. Did shorter subjects walk with greater tortuosity than taller ones on the same terrain? Did shorter subjects take relatively more steps even after normalizing for leg length? A possible comparison would be (number of steps)*(leg length)/(start to end distance). I feel that the evidence from this study is not that strong.

Although it is a strength of this study that so much can be learned from pure observation, that does not mean controlled conditions are not scientifically helpful. As mentioned earlier, a helpful control could have been to ask subjects to walk straighter but less preferred paths on the same terrain, treating human paths as an independent variable. Another would be to treat terrain as an independent variable, by using level ground and intermediate terrain conditions. This would make it easier to test whether taller subjects walk straighter ahead on more uneven terrain than shorter subjects. Indeed, the data set already includes some patches of flatter terrain, not included here. Additional and simpler tests might be possible based on existing data.

Conclusion

This is an ambitious undertaking, presenting a wealth of unprecedented data to quantitatively test basic ecological questions that have long been unanswered. There are a number of considerable strengths that merit appreciation, especially the ability to quantitatively predict when humans will walk more circuitously. The weaknesses are about limitations in the conclusions that can be drawn thus far rather than the correctness of the study. I consider this to be a first step that will hopefully enable and inspire a long line of future work that will address these questions more in depth.

The systematic way in which path selection is parametrically investigated is the main contribution.

Strengths:

The authors have developed an impressive workflow to study gait and gaze in natural terrain. They are able to determine footholds and gaze points in the 3D world, and explore different path selections in the terrain.

Weaknesses:

The finding that walkers prefer less tortuous, demanding paths is hardly surprising, and from the data it is still not clear what actual visual features are used to choose among alternative routes or what the nature of the decision process is. The authors discuss energetic cost and other "factors" that might influence path selection, but as yet there is no way to express these ideas rigorously in such complex natural settings.

results.result: The photogrammetry-based terrain reconstruction method produces reliable 3D reconstructions with median errors of 4.5 cm overall and 4.0 cm at foothold locations, representing less than 20% of average foot length.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 provide convergent evidence for reconstruction reliability through quantitative mesh comparison analysis. The median errors (C17, C18) are contextualized against average foot length (C19), and the interpretation (C20) is mathematically sound. The validation approach using multiple traversals of the same terrain is appropriate.

results.result: A convolutional neural network trained on retinocentric depth images can predict foothold locations above chance (median AUC > 0.5 for all subjects), demonstrating that depth information contributes to foothold selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C13 and C21-C23 collectively demonstrate that depth features predict foothold locations. The CNN analysis shows above-chance performance across all subjects (C22), supporting the inference that depth information plays a role in foothold finding (C23). The experimental design appropriately tests the hypothesis using held-out terrain.

results.result: Walkers prefer flatter paths, with chosen path slopes (mean 9.5°) significantly lower than simulated viable alternatives (mean 14.9°), indicating intentional selection of paths that minimize height changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C14 and C28-C34 provide strong statistical evidence (t(8)=7.64, p<<0.001; C33) that walkers choose flatter paths than terrain constraints alone would predict. The simulation approach appropriately controls for viable alternatives. However, the claim of 'intentional' behavior (C69) is an inference that goes beyond what the data directly show—the preference could reflect learned heuristics rather than conscious planning.

results.result: Walkers choose more tortuous (curved) paths when straight alternatives involve steeper slopes, demonstrating a trade-off between path directness and flatness to avoid height changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C15, and C37-C43 demonstrate a systematic relationship between path tortuosity and straight-path slope across all subjects (C42, C45). The data show walkers take increasingly curved paths as the slope of straight alternatives increases. However, C38 is labeled as a hypothesis, and the causal interpretation (C43, C70) involves inference beyond direct observation. The pattern is consistent but individual variability is high.

results.result: The strength of the slope-tortuosity trade-off varies with leg length, with shorter-legged individuals showing stronger correlations (r=-0.83, p=0.005), suggesting body-specific sensorimotor decision-making.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 report a significant negative correlation between leg length and slope-tortuosity correlation strength. However, C48 contains an apparent error (correlation values reported in cm rather than as coefficients), raising concerns about data reporting accuracy. The sample size (n=9) is small for detecting individual differences, and the correlation, while statistically significant, is based on aggregated per-subject measures. The inference to body-specific decision-making (C60-C61) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Walkers plan ahead to select flatter paths and plan individual foothold locations, as evidenced by their choice of indirect routes that avoid height changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C71-C72 infer planning from observed path selection behavior. While the data show walkers choose paths that avoid height changes (supporting claims), the inference of 'planning ahead' is not directly demonstrated. The study does not measure planning horizon or provide direct evidence of prospective path evaluation. The conclusion relies on the assumption that the observed behavior requires planning rather than reactive or learned responses.

results.result: Locomotor behavior in natural terrain is controlled by decision mechanisms that account for multiple factors including sensory information, motor constraints, energetic costs, and path planning.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C5, and C84 represent the overarching conclusion synthesizing multiple analyses. The evidence from depth information (C13-C23), path slope preferences (C14, C28-C34), and tortuosity-slope trade-offs (C42-C43) collectively support multi-factor decision-making. However, the specific contribution of each factor and their relative weighting remain unquantified. The conclusion is well-supported as a qualitative framework but lacks a quantitative model.

results.result: The photogrammetry-based terrain reconstruction method enables more precise analysis of visually guided walking than previous approaches by eliminating parallax error and IMU drift.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 and C103 describe methodological advantages. The elimination of parallax error (from flat-ground assumptions) and IMU drift (through terrain-based registration) are valid improvements. However, the claim of 'greater precision' (C53) is not quantitatively validated against previous methods—only the reconstruction reliability is assessed (C16-C20). The methodological contribution is clear but comparative precision claims are not directly tested.

results.result: Despite the complexity of natural terrain, walkers show consistent path selection patterns across individuals and repeated traversals, suggesting terrain features systematically influence path choice.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 and C82 describe observed regularities in path selection. Visual inspection (Figure 3) and quantitative analyses support consistency. However, the degree of consistency is not quantified, and the claim that 'terrain features serve as a basis' (C57) is an inference. The evidence supports systematic influences but does not identify which specific features drive consistency.

results.result: The preference for flatter paths is likely driven by energetic costs of stepping up and down, suggesting walkers minimize energy expenditure in natural terrain.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C66 propose energetic optimization as the mechanism underlying path preferences. While this interpretation is plausible and consistent with prior work on flat terrain (C24-C25, C63-C65), the study does not measure energy expenditure. The inference is reasonable but speculative—other factors like stability, injury risk, or cognitive load could also explain the preference for flatter paths.

results.result: The planning horizon for natural terrain walking may differ from laboratory studies (5 steps vs. 8-9 steps), potentially due to terrain complexity, visual working memory demands, or peripheral vision use.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C79 discuss planning horizons but are largely speculative (C73, C78, C79). The comparison between studies (C74-C76) highlights discrepancies but the current study does not directly measure planning horizon. The discussion appropriately identifies uncertainty but does not resolve it. This represents speculation about future work rather than a supported finding.

results.result: The dataset comprises 9 participants (5 male, 4 female, ages 23-54, leg lengths 81-103.5 cm) who completed 4230 total steps across two study sites (Austin and Berkeley).
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C93 provide demographic and dataset characteristics. These are directly reported descriptive statistics with no interpretation required. The information is clearly stated and internally consistent.

results.result: Data were collected using a Pupil Labs eye tracker (120 Hz eye tracking, 30 Hz scene camera) and Motion Shadow motion capture suit (100 Hz, 17 IMUs) while participants walked natural terrain trails.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C99 describe equipment specifications and experimental procedures. These are straightforward methodological details that are clearly stated and appropriate for the study design.

results.result: The observed variability in path selection likely reflects learned heuristics rather than strict optimization criteria, allowing flexible path selection.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 proposes that variability reflects learned heuristics. This is speculative interpretation of the observed variance in the data. While the high variability (noted in per-path-segment analysis) is inconsistent with strict optimization, the inference to 'learned heuristics' is not directly tested. Alternative explanations (e.g., stochastic decision-making, context-dependent weighting) are not ruled out.

results.result: The reconstruction and integration procedures should be generally useful for analyzing visually guided behavior in natural environments.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 speculates about broader applicability of the methods. While the approach is novel and potentially useful, generalizability to other behaviors or environments is not demonstrated. This represents a reasonable expectation but not a tested result.

results.result: The terrain reconstruction procedure produces reliable 3D reconstructions with median errors of 4.5 cm overall and 4.0 cm at foothold locations, with 95% of errors below 20 cm, representing less than 20% of average foot length.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently praised the technical achievement and methodological advances. One reviewer stated the work is 'methodologically, very impressive' and another noted 'the technical achievement is impressive' and 'the team managed to collect and analyze an unprecedented, one-of-a-kind dataset.' The reconstruction accuracy was not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Retinocentric depth information is predictive of foothold selection, as demonstrated by a CNN that predicted foothold locations above chance (median AUC above 0.5 for all subjects) from depth images.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly stated 'There is also good evidence for the third question, showing that retinocentric depth is predictive of chosen footholds' and noted 'The results are strong.' Another reviewer confirmed 'they show using a neural network model that participants could choose the footholds based on their sensory (visual) information about depth.' No concerns were raised about this finding.

results.result: Walkers prefer flatter paths, with chosen path slopes (median 9.5°) significantly lower than simulated random paths (median 14.9°), a difference of 5.56° that was statistically significant (t(8)=7.64, p<<0.001).
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the finding, one reviewer expressed significant concerns about the simulation methodology, stating 'I was not entirely convinced by the evidence for the second...question' and 'I don't find this especially strong evidence that the chosen paths were indeed relatively flatter. I would prefer to be convinced by hard data than by unequal simulations.' The reviewer was confused about how simulations were constructed and questioned whether the comparison was 'apples-to-apples.'

results.result: Walkers change direction to avoid steeper paths, choosing more tortuous (indirect) routes when straight-ahead paths have greater slopes, demonstrating a trade-off between path directness and flatness.
results.evaluation: One reviewer stated 'I consider the evidence strongest for the first of the main questions. The results show subjects walking with more laterally deviating paths, measured by a quantity called "tortuosity," when the direct straight-ahead paths appear to have steeper ups and downs.' However, the same reviewer objected to the causal language 'TO AVOID,' suggesting it 'implies a degree of intent not evident in the data' and preferring the interpretation that 'walkers changed direction more when straight-ahead paths seemed to have steeper height changes.'

results.result: Path selection behavior is body-specific, with shorter-legged subjects showing stronger correlations between straight path slope and tortuosity (r=-0.83, p=0.005), suggesting they are more likely to choose longer, flatter paths when faced with steep terrain.
results.evaluation: One reviewer expressed substantial doubts about this finding, stating 'I had some misgivings about the fourth question' and 'I still have doubts.' The reviewer noted that 'Figure 18 provides more detail of the underlying data, with considerably lower correlations' and suspected 'Figure 10 benefits from some statistical artifacts due to binning and other operations.' The reviewer also questioned the theoretical basis, asking 'Shouldn't all subjects equally avoid steep angles, regardless of their dimensional height?' and concluded 'I feel that the evidence from this study is not that strong.'

results.result: Walkers plan ahead to select paths, as evidenced by their choice of indirect routes to achieve flatter paths, demonstrating that planning is an important component of path selection in rugged terrain.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the evidence for planning behavior. One reviewer noted the study addresses 'how far people look to decide where to step' and another stated the authors 'find that paths are chosen that are consistently less steep and deviate from the straight line more than an average random path, suggesting that participants indeed trade off steepness for path length.' The planning inference from choosing indirect routes was not directly challenged.

results.result: Walkers take terrain structure into account when selecting paths, with locomotor behavior controlled by decision mechanisms that account for multiple factors including sensory and motor information, costs, and path planning.
results.evaluation: The editor stated 'The evidence supporting the conclusions is overall compelling' and one reviewer noted 'the ability to quantitatively predict when humans will walk more circuitously' as a strength. However, one reviewer noted 'from the data it is still not clear what actual visual features are used to choose among alternative routes or what the nature of the decision process is,' indicating the mechanisms remain somewhat unclear despite the overall pattern being accepted.

results.result: The terrain reconstruction and integration procedures represent methodological advances that allow greater precision than previous studies and enable quantitative examination of how visual environment structure influences foothold selection.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously praised the methodological contributions. One stated 'Methodologically, the work is very impressive and presents a further step forward towards understanding real-world locomotion.' Another noted 'The technical achievement is impressive' and 'This team managed to collect and analyze an unprecedented, one-of-a-kind dataset.' The editor described it as a 'fundamental study' that 'opens up new approaches to studying (visually guided) behavior in natural settings outside the lab.'

results.result: There are regularities in the paths chosen by walkers, both across individuals and across repeats of the same walk, suggesting that terrain features serve as a basis for path choice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these observational findings without challenge. One reviewer noted 'the systematic way in which path selection is parametrically investigated is the main contribution' and another stated the study presents 'multiple ways to visualize and quantify the rich and complex natural behavior.' The regularities were accepted as part of the overall pattern of findings.

results.result: The preference for flatter paths is likely driven by energetic costs of stepping up or down, with walkers potentially adjusting behavior to minimize energetic costs in natural outdoor terrains.
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not directly challenge this interpretation, one noted 'The authors discuss energetic cost and other "factors" that might influence path selection, but as yet there is no way to express these ideas rigorously in such complex natural settings.' This suggests the energetic cost explanation remains speculative and not rigorously demonstrated, though it is a reasonable interpretation of the observed behavior.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on depth features predicting foothold locations (C13, C21-C23). Both evaluations find the CNN analysis and evidence compelling, with OpenEval rating SUPPORTED and peer reviewers explicitly stating 'There is also good evidence' and 'The results are strong.'

Both support the overarching multi-factor decision-making conclusion (C1, C5, C84). OpenEval notes the qualitative framework is well-supported but lacks quantitative modeling. Peer reviewers find evidence 'overall compelling' but note 'it is still not clear what actual visual features are used,' indicating similar recognition of both strengths and limitations.

Both support observed regularities in path selection (C56, C57, C82). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED while noting consistency is not quantified. Peer reviewers accept these observational findings without challenge, acknowledging the systematic investigation as a main contribution.

Both rate energetic optimization claims (C62, C66) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes the interpretation is plausible but speculative without energy expenditure measurements. Peer reviewers similarly note 'there is no way to express these ideas rigorously in such complex natural settings.'

Strong agreement on reconstruction reliability (C16-C18, C20). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval validates the quantitative mesh comparison approach. Peer reviewers consistently praised the technical achievement as 'methodologically, very impressive' with no concerns about reconstruction accuracy.

Disagreement on path flatness preference (C14, C28-C34, C68). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on strong statistical evidence (t(8)=7.64, p<<0.001) but notes inference about 'intentional' behavior. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, with one stating 'I was not entirely convinced' and questioning whether simulations provide 'apples-to-apples' comparison.

Disagreement on planning inference (C3, C4, C71, C72). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting planning is not directly demonstrated and could reflect reactive responses. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, accepting that choosing indirect routes demonstrates planning without directly challenging this inference.

Both strongly support methodological contributions (C53-C55, C103, C80). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but notes comparative precision claims lack direct testing. Peer reviewers unanimously praised the work as 'unprecedented' and 'a fundamental study' that 'opens up new approaches.'

Both support tortuosity-slope relationship (C2, C15, C37-C43, C70) but with reservations. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED while noting causal interpretation involves inference and high individual variability. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED but object to causal language 'TO AVOID' as implying 'intent not evident in the data.'

Strong agreement on uncertainty regarding leg length correlation (C49, C50, C60). Both rate UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes apparent data reporting error (C48), small sample size, and speculative inference. Peer reviewers express 'substantial doubts,' questioning statistical artifacts and theoretical basis, concluding 'evidence from this study is not that strong.'

OpenEval evaluates planning horizon discussion (C73-C79) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is largely speculative and represents future work rather than supported findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval rates demographic and dataset characteristics (C85-C93) as SUPPORTED, noting these are straightforward descriptive statistics. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological details.

OpenEval rates equipment specifications and procedures (C94-C99) as SUPPORTED, describing them as clearly stated methodological details. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these technical specifications.

OpenEval rates learned heuristics interpretation (C52) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is speculative and alternative explanations are not ruled out. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific interpretive claim.

OpenEval rates broader applicability speculation (C80) as UNCERTAIN, noting generalizability is not demonstrated. While peer reviewers praised methodological contributions including C80 in R8, they did not separately evaluate this forward-looking claim about applicability.
